title: Feedback that lands

audience.who: new and mid-level people managers in a corporate office; busy, sceptical of training videos
audience.knows: what giving and receiving feedback feels like; probably no named method for it
audience.cares_about: getting one piece of work fixed without a defensive conversation or a damaged working relationship

outcome: Before their next one-to-one, the manager can turn a concern about one piece of a report's work into a short conversation: the situation, the specific behaviour, its impact, then a question and an agreed next step
through_line: Feedback gets heard when it is about one specific thing the person did and what it caused, said soon, and ends in a question; a vague verdict gets defended against

arc_plan.what: After a short presenter opening, Maya, the manager, gives her report a vague verdict on one piece of work in passing, days late; the report defends and nothing changes. Framed as invented.
Name the four moves as common workplace practice, not research: situation, specific behaviour, impact, then ask and agree a next step; held as one short sequence the viewer can carry
The same moment replayed: Maya uses the four moves on the same piece of work, soon after it; each move is marked as it lands and the report shifts from defending to discussing
Pause and predict: the viewer sees Maya's tempting wrong line and picks which move fixes it before she shows it; then the viewer picks one piece of work from their own week to use it on
Back to the outcome in one breath: one specific thing, said soon, ending in a question; the presenter closes by handing the viewer their next one-to-one

must_cover.what: the four moves, in order: describe the situation, the specific behaviour, its impact, then ask and agree a next step
feedback on one piece of work, given soon after it rather than saved up
the ask: the report's view is invited before the next step is agreed, so it is a conversation, not a verdict
the method presented as a common workplace practice, never as a research finding
describing behaviour versus judging the person, as the knowledge sheet states it
why a vague or judgemental verdict tends to be defended against, as the knowledge sheet states it

must_avoid: statistics, percentages or research claims unless the knowledge stage sources them
lecturing, a teacher-like tone, or telling the viewer they have been doing it wrong
perfect characters: Maya gets it wrong first
stereotypes of managers or reports, including gender or age
a cartoony register: mascots, dot eyes, glow, bouncy motion
the presenter inside the scenario; bookends only
a list of tips in place of the four moves
HR, disciplinary or formal performance processes
example_posture: One invented, ordinary piece of office work (say, a client update that went out unclear), framed as illustrative; Maya is the manager and the report stays plain and unnamed unless the requester decides otherwise; no real company, no industry jargon, no drama, no raised voices.
visual_direction: Grown-up and plain. A code-drawn presenter only at the opening and the close. Inside, dialogue scenes between Maya (an illustrated woman in her 30s, office clothes) and her report (a simpler code-drawn figure, or seen from behind) at a desk or small meeting room; the same moment replayed with the change at each move marked; Maya's thoughts as a quiet aside while she chooses her words; the four moves as a short checklist that builds once and returns at practice and payoff. Muted colour, restrained motion, generous space.
voice_note: A colleague who has had these conversations and got some wrong; plain, direct, a little dry, never teacher-like or cheerleading. Say each point once; these viewers notice padding.
open_questions: Should the report have a name, or stay unnamed?
Is there an organisation-specific feedback policy or form to align with? None was given, so the lesson stays generic.
Length is 5 to 7 minutes (planned 6); the practice segment is the one to stretch or shrink.

look.note: From the user (Kshitij): plain, mature, non-cartoony; this lesson tests whether Loom can look grown-up. No glow, no mascots. A code-drawn presenter opens and closes the lesson, bookends only, with no invented name. Inside, Maya, an illustrated woman in her 30s in office clothes, plays the manager who gives feedback; the report can be a simpler code-drawn figure or seen from behind.

inferred: visual_direction (beyond the people and look answers)
